title.raw: Simple Energy raises ₹1,750 crore as TVS and Bajaj lead e-scooters
title.rendered: Simple Energy raises ₹1,750 crore as TVS and Bajaj lead e-scooters

content.raw:
Bengaluru electric scooter maker Simple Energy has raised ₹1,750 crore (about $182 million) in an all-equity Series C round led by the family office of Thyrocare founder Dr Arokiaswamy Velumani, Entrackr reported on 30 September 2026. It was the largest Indian startup round of the week and of the July–September quarter. The money will pay for a new factory and a wider sales network as Simple tries to grow from a niche brand into a mass-market player.

Key takeaways

  • The ₹1,750 crore round is Simple Energy's largest. It takes total funding to about ₹2,530 crore ($263 million), according to Entrackr. (One crore is 10 million rupees.)
  • Simple delivered 10,429 scooters from January to August 2026, up 203% on a year earlier, but still sells only about 1,500 a month, Autocar Professional reported.
  • India's electric two-wheeler market grew 85% year on year to 2,03,411 registrations in September 2026. Legacy manufacturers TVS and Bajaj together held about half the market.
  • The round accounted for most of the money Indian startups raised in the week of 28 September to 3 October, which totalled $233.6 million by Inc42's count and $411.5 million by Entrackr's.

The round: who invested and why it is unusual

The investor list is short and has no venture capital firms on it. Velumani's family office led, joined by Haran Family Office, Bengaluru-based investor Amit Mishra, founder and CEO Suhas Rajkumar and co-founder and CFO Ankit Gupta, according to Inc42 and Entrackr. Inc42 put the round at about $180 million and total equity raised at about $264 million. The small gap with Entrackr's figures comes from the exchange rate used.

A round this large with no venture fund among its investors stands out. A family office (a private firm that invests one wealthy family's money) does not have to return capital to outside investors on a fund's timetable, which can suit a business that has to build factories before they earn money. Founders putting their own money into the round is also a signal of conviction.

Before this round, Simple raised money in smaller steps, according to Entrackr:

DateRoundAmount
November 2021Pre-Series A$21 million
February 2023Bridge$20 million+
July 2024Series A$20 million
September 2025Bridge$10 million
June 2026Debt and equity₹250 crore
September 2026Series C₹1,750 crore (~$182 million)

The Series C alone is larger than all its earlier funding combined: about ₹780 crore of the ₹2,530 crore total came before it.

Where the money goes

Simple says it will use the money for a new manufacturing facility, more production capacity, a larger sales, distribution and service network, hiring, research and development for its next products, marketing and its supply chain. Rajkumar summed up the priorities as "a new manufacturing facility, higher production, an expanded distribution and service network" and the next generation of products, Inc42 reported.

The production numbers need care. Coverage of the round put Simple's capacity at 10,000 units a month. Earlier in September, Inc42 reported that Simple was making about 3,000 scooters a month, selling about 1,500, and aiming for 10,000 a month by March 2027. The 10,000 figure is best read as a target the new factory is meant to deliver, not current output.

Retail is the other bottleneck. Simple had around 80–90 stores in about 60 cities in September, depending on the report, and plans 160–170 by March 2027, according to Inc42. Scooter buyers in India want to test-ride and get servicing nearby, so a small store network limits sales.

The products: from premium to family scooters

Simple Energy was founded in 2019 by Suhas Rajkumar and Shreshth Mishra, and became known for the Simple One, a long-range performance scooter. Its range now includes the One, OneS and Ultra. On 25 September 2026 it began deliveries of the Wave, a family scooter priced from ₹1.10 lakh (₹110,000) ex-showroom, according to Autocar Professional. The Wave comes with batteries from 2.2 kWh to 5 kWh and a claimed range of 110 km to 243 km under India's IDC test cycle.

The Wave enters the most crowded part of the market. Ola Electric's S1Z sells at ₹79,999 to ₹99,999 and Ather's Konarc starts at ₹99,999, according to an Inc42 analysis, so Simple's entry model costs more than both. The company says it is the first Indian manufacturer to use motors free of heavy rare-earth materials, Entrackr reported.

How big is Simple Energy today?

Simple is growing fast from a small base:

  • Sales: 10,429 units in January–August 2026, against 3,436 a year earlier. Its best month was March 2026 with 1,780 units. It sold 1,508 in August, down from 1,666 in July, according to Inc42.
  • Rank: 13th among electric two-wheeler makers in calendar 2025, rising to about ninth on average through August 2026, according to Autocar Professional.
  • Revenue: About ₹171 crore in FY26 (April 2025 to March 2026), up from ₹44 crore in FY25, according to Inc42. Entrackr put FY26 revenue at ₹150–160 crore against ₹40 crore. Audited figures were not published with the round.

For comparison, the total market registered 1,82,078 electric two-wheelers in August, so Simple's 1,508 units were less than 1% of it. The new capital is meant to change that, but the gap with market leaders selling 50,000 a month is very large.

Costs are also rising. Rajkumar told Inc42 that commodity prices had risen roughly 25–30% over the previous two quarters, which squeezes margins across the industry.

The Indian electric two-wheeler market in September 2026

Simple raised money in a growing market. Electric two-wheeler registrations on the government's Vahan database rose 85% year on year to 2,03,411 in September, and electric models made up 11.4% of all two-wheeler registrations, Autocar Professional reported. Registrations for April–September 2026 reached 11,08,606, up 73%, and the market is on course to pass 2 million in FY27.

MakerSeptember 2026 unitsShareYoY change
TVS Motor53,98926.5%+126%
Bajaj Auto48,38323.8%+139%
Ather Energy30,47715.0%+57%
Hero MotoCorp (Vida)24,30511.9%+83%
Ola Electric13,4496.6%-3%

Source: Autocar Professional, based on Vahan data. EVreporter's count, also from Vahan, put September at 207,314 units and 11.6% penetration. Small differences between trackers are normal because Vahan data is updated for several days after each month ends.

The clearest trend is consolidation around established manufacturers. TVS and Bajaj held 49% of registrations in April–September, up from about 42% a year earlier. Ola Electric's share fell to 7.7% from 17.4%. Among smaller players, River Mobility (5,549 units in September) and Greaves Electric (9,317) grew fast. Startups can still win share, but legacy makers with large dealer networks are taking most of the new demand.

The funding picture: first week of October

Simple's round dominated an otherwise quiet week. The two main trackers count it differently.

  • Inc42 counted $233.6 million across 16 deals from 28 September to 2 October, up 14.9% from the previous week, with deal count down 23.8%. Simple accounted for about 77% of the total.
  • Entrackr counted $411.46 million across 24 startups from 28 September to 3 October, more than double the previous week's $188.49 million. Its total includes a $150 million round for SiMa.ai, a physical-AI startup, which Inc42's list did not include.

Other notable deals that week included home-interiors startup Gravity ($15 million, led by 3one4 Capital and Info Edge Ventures), lender Seeds Fincap (about $10.4 million Series B led by the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation), agritech Balwaan Krishi (about $10.4 million Series B) and edtech Arivihan (about $10.2 million Series A led by Accel and Prosus), according to Inc42. Bengaluru accounted for 13 of Entrackr's 24 deals. ITC also completed its purchase of Yoga Bar's parent, and seed fund WEH Ventures announced the first close of its third fund, which targets ₹250 crore.

Over the July–September quarter, Indian startups raised about $2.9 billion, according to Entrackr, slightly above $2.78 billion a year earlier but below Q1 2026 ($3.87 billion) and Q2 ($3.5 billion). EV startups raised $583 million, second only to AI at $635.3 million. Simple's round was the quarter's largest, and River Mobility's $120 million ranked fourth. Track rounds as they happen on our funding tracker.

Why it matters

Simple Energy now has the capital to test whether a startup can still break into an Indian EV scooter market that legacy manufacturers increasingly control. The bet is that a family scooter, more stores and a larger factory can turn about 1,500 sales a month into several times that. The risks are clear: the Wave costs more than rival entry models, input costs are rising, and Ola Electric's loss of share shows how quickly a startup's position can weaken. For investors, the round shows that patient private capital is willing to back Indian EV manufacturing in a year when quarterly startup funding has been falling. More EV and startup coverage is in our news section.

Who led Simple Energy's funding round?

The family office of Dr Arokiaswamy Velumani, the founder of diagnostics company Thyrocare. Haran Family Office, investor Amit Mishra and Simple's founders also took part.

How many scooters does Simple Energy sell?

It delivered 10,429 units from January to August 2026, about 1,500 a month recently, according to Vahan data reported by Autocar Professional and Inc42.

Who leads India's electric two-wheeler market?

In September 2026, TVS Motor led with 26.5% of registrations, followed by Bajaj Auto (23.8%), Ather Energy (15%), Hero MotoCorp's Vida (11.9%) and Ola Electric (6.6%), according to Autocar Professional.

What is the Simple Wave's price?

It starts at ₹1.10 lakh ex-showroom, with deliveries from 25 September 2026.
